summary.text: Taking the universally quantified statement at \(n=0\), the divisor sums and totient contribution give \(a(0)=0\). But \(0\neq1\) and \(0\) is not prime, contradicting the asserted characterization of the zeros.

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
\sigma_1(n)=\sum_{d\mid n}d,\qquad \sigma_2(n)=\sum_{d\mid n}d^2,
\]
and let \(\varphi(n)\) denote Euler's totient. In the statement being disproved, these functions are extended to \(n=0\) by taking the finite set of divisors of \(0\) to be empty and by setting \(\varphi(0)=0\). The value of the sequence is then defined by
\[
a(n)=\operatorname{toNat}\bigl(\sigma_2(n)+\varphi(n)\sigma_1(n)-2n^2\bigr),
\]
where \(\operatorname{toNat}(m)=m\) for a nonnegative integer \(m\), and is \(0\) for a negative integer. We will only apply it to the integer \(0\), so no truncation issue arises.

The universal assertion under consideration is
\[
\forall n\in\mathbb N,\quad
\bigl(a(n)=0\iff n=1\text{ or }n\text{ is prime}\bigr)
\quad\text{and}\quad
\bigl(a(n)=2\iff n=pq\text{ for two distinct primes }p,q\bigr).
\]
There is no condition \(n\ge 1\) in this universally quantified statement. We disprove it by taking \(n=0\).

Under the stated zero conventions, the divisor set of \(0\) is empty. Hence both divisor sums are empty sums and therefore equal to zero:
\[
\sigma_1(0)=\sum_{d\in\varnothing}d=0,
\qquad
\sigma_2(0)=\sum_{d\in\varnothing}d^2=0.
\]
Also \(\varphi(0)=0\), and of course \(0^2=0\). Consequently the integer inside the definition of \(a(0)\) is
\[
\sigma_2(0)+\varphi(0)\sigma_1(0)-2\cdot0^2
 =0+0\cdot0-0=0.
\]
Since converting the nonnegative integer \(0\) to a natural number again gives \(0\), it follows that
\[
a(0)=0.
\]

Now examine the first claimed equivalence at \(n=0\). Its left-hand side, \(a(0)=0\), is true. Its right-hand side is
\[
0=1\quad\text{or}\quad 0\text{ is prime}.
\]
Both alternatives are false: \(0\ne1\), and \(0\) is not prime (in particular, every prime is at least \(2\)). Thus the right-hand side is false. Therefore
\[
a(0)=0\not\iff \bigl(0=1\text{ or }0\text{ is prime}\bigr).
\]
So the first equivalence already fails at \(n=0\). The conjunction containing it is consequently false at \(n=0\), irrespective of the second equivalence concerning the value \(2\). Hence the displayed assertion quantified over every natural number is false.

This counterexample depends essentially on the missing positivity hypothesis. The canonical OEIS conjecture is stated only for \(n\ge1\); \(n=0\) is outside that domain. Accordingly, this argument disproves the unguarded all-natural-numbers formulation above, but by itself it does not disprove the original positive-integer conjecture.
